prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: For, Robert, Philen

outputs.L1:
**For Robert Philen**

You are like me: you, too, will die—but not today. You, incommensurate, make the hours shine. If I say to you, “To you I say,” you have not been set to music or broadcast live on the ghost radio; you may never be an oil painting or an Old Master’s charcoal sketch. You are a concordance of person, number, voice, and place, strawberries scattered through your name as though they were budding shrubs. How you remind me of some spring, its waters cool and clear—late rain clinging to your leaves, shaken by a light wind—which is where you occur, in grassy moonlight.

And you are a lily, an aster, white trillium or viburnum, by all rights mine: a white star in the meadow sky, the snow still returning from its earthward journeys, here where there is no snow. (I dreamed the snow was you, when there was snow.) You are my right; you have come to be my night. Your body takes on the dimensions of sleep; the shape of sleep becomes you.

And you fall from the sky with several flowers. Words spill from your mouth in waves; your lips taste like the sea, salt-sweet. Trees and seas have flown away: I call it loving you. Home is nowhere; therefore, you—a kind of dwelling and welcome, a song after all, and free of any Eden we can name.
outputs.L2:
**For Robert Philen**

You resemble me in this: death awaits you too, though not on this day. Because you cannot be measured, the hours glow. When I tell you, “I am speaking to you,” no melody has claimed you, no phantom radio has carried you live; perhaps you will never become an oil portrait or a charcoal drawing by an Old Master. Instead, you gather person, number, voice, and place into harmony. Strawberries seem scattered through your name like bushes beginning to bloom.

You call to mind a certain spring, its water cold and transparent, with late rain resting on your leaves and a faint wind trembling through them. There, in moonlit grass, is where you appear. You are lily and aster, white trillium and viburnum—rightfully mine—a pale star in the meadow’s heavens. Snow continues returning from its journeys toward the earth, even here, where none exists. When snow did exist, I dreamed it was you.

You are what is due to me, and you have become my night. Your body expands into the proportions of sleep, while sleep itself assumes your form. You descend from the sky accompanied by several blossoms. Language pours from your mouth like surf, and your lips carry the sea’s mingled sweetness and salt. The forests and oceans have taken flight; I name that disappearance loving you.

There is no place that can be called home. For that reason, you become a kind of dwelling and reception—a song, finally, untouched by any Eden we are able to name.
outputs.L3:
The speaker begins by acknowledging a shared human reality: both he and Robert Philen are mortal, and death will eventually come for them. Yet that end does not belong to the present moment. For now, life and love remain immediate, allowing the speaker to celebrate Robert’s presence rather than dwell on mortality.

Robert is portrayed as entirely unique, someone whose essence cannot be captured through conventional forms of representation. Neither music nor broadcasting, neither painting nor drawing, can adequately convey who he is. Instead, the speaker turns to the natural world for a language rich enough to suggest Robert’s beauty. Images of spring, flowers, moonlight, snow, and water create a vivid portrait of freshness, radiance, purity, and fluidity. Nature does not simply resemble Robert; it appears intimately connected to him, as though its beauty were an extension of his being.

The speaker’s love deepens this connection by transforming Robert into elemental and intimate experiences. Robert becomes night and sleep, suggesting rest, trust, and closeness; he becomes the sea, evoking depth, movement, and physical immersion; and he becomes song, embodying emotion in its most direct and expressive form. Through these transformations, love dissolves the boundaries between the beloved, the speaker, and the surrounding world.

Finally, the poem presents Robert as a refuge in a world where home cannot be securely located. When home is nowhere, Robert himself becomes a place of dwelling—a source of welcome, belonging, and freedom. This sanctuary cannot be reduced to any fixed image of paradise. It exists beyond definition, created through love and shared presence. Thus, Robert is not merely someone the speaker loves; he becomes the speaker’s deepest sense of home.
outputs.L4:
The poem addresses Robert Philen directly, turning an intimate encounter with the beloved into a meditation on mortality, love, and displacement. Its lush imagery—flowers blooming and fading, snow covering the world, the sea suggesting distance and motion, sleep resembling both rest and death, and song preserving what time threatens to erase—places human affection within a landscape of beauty and impermanence. Every image carries a double significance: nature is radiant, yet transient; sleep offers refuge, yet hints at oblivion; the sea opens a path toward elsewhere while also emphasizing separation and exile.

Against this uncertainty, the beloved becomes a source of stability. Home is no longer defined by geography, origin, or even the promise of paradise. Instead, it is found in the presence of another person. The direct address to Robert Philen gives the poem the closeness of a private declaration, as though speaking the beloved’s name could resist loss and preserve intimacy. Love cannot abolish death or restore a permanently secure place, but it can make a fragile life inhabitable. Through affection, memory, and song, transience acquires radiance and meaning. The poem ultimately suggests that the deepest refuge is not a distant destination but the bond between two people—a sustaining home carried within love itself.

### For Robert Philen

For Robert Philen, every challenge was an opportunity to learn, grow, and inspire others. His curiosity and determination shaped the way he approached both work and life. Rather than seeking recognition, Robert valued meaningful relationships, thoughtful ideas, and lasting contributions. His story reminds us that genuine success is measured not only by personal achievements, but also by the positive influence we have on the people around us.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a lyrical prose poem dedicated to Robert Philen that meditates on mortality, love, language, nature, and the beloved as a form of home.
counterfactuals.output:
**For Robert Philen**

We are given only a little weather: a handful of mornings, rain darkening the bark, light loosening its gold across the floor. The body knows this and keeps its quiet calendar—each breath a small leaf opening, each heartbeat already practicing farewell. Still, Robert, love asks us to live as if the hour were not vanishing, but arriving.

What can language do against the dark? Nothing, perhaps, but strike its match. A name spoken tenderly becomes a window. A sentence, if held long enough, warms in the hands. We say *river*, and something in us begins to move; we say *bird*, and the air remembers its wings; we say *beloved*, and the mortal world, for one astonished moment, is not a place we must leave.

Outside, the grasses bow to what cannot be seen. Pines lift their green fires into evening. The moon, faithful to its disappearances, teaches that absence may be another form of return. Even the fallen apple sweetens the ground. Even the stone gathers moss, that soft alphabet of rain.

Perhaps this is all home ever was: not walls, but recognition. The face that turns toward us when we enter. The voice that finds us across distance. The hand whose touch makes the body less a boundary than a door. To love another is to dwell briefly beyond oneself, to set a lamp in the window of another life and call that brightness ours.

And when the last word loosens from the tongue, when the path bends past the trees and out of sight, may love remain—not as an answer, but as the place where all our questions rested. May the beloved be the earth beneath us, the roof of stars above, the room in which even silence knows our name.

For we are passing, yes. But while we pass, we shelter one another. And sometimes, Robert, that shelter is so deep, so tenderly made, it feels like forever.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose an experimental romantic poem beginning “For Robert Philen” and incorporating flowers, snow, moonlight, sleep, the sea, and the phrase “ghost radio.”
counterfactuals.output:
For Robert Philen

I leave the flowers unfastened  
at the throat of morning—  
wild vowels, blue bells,  
a rose rehearsing your name.

Snow enters quietly,  
an erased letter  
the sky keeps sending.

Under moonlight  
our shadows overlap  
like two pages soaked through,  
like sleep dreaming itself  
inside another sleep.

Far off, the sea  
turns its silver machinery,  
each wave translating absence  
into touch, touch, touch—

and from the dark window  
a ghost radio murmurs  
the weather of vanished stars.

Come closer.

Even silence has a pulse  
when you are near;  
even winter opens  
its white hands.

I tune my body toward yours—  
all static, salt, and blossom—  
until love is the only station  
left in the world.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a single-paragraph prose poem in a lush, surreal, contemporary style. Address the beloved directly, use parenthetical asides and grammatical imagery, and end with the idea that love is a song beyond Eden.
counterfactuals.output: Beloved, you arrive through the blue notification of dawn carrying rain in your pockets, and suddenly the city grows antlers of glass, every window trembling with small captive oceans; I speak your name and the vowels open like night-blooming flowers (the consonants, shy animals, drink from their shadows), while between us a comma kneels, bright and breathless, asking the sentence not to end. You touch my wrist and time forgets its password; elevators rise into orchards, satellites shed silver feathers, and all the traffic lights turn green for the ghosts we might have been. Stay, even if staying is only a verb with its coat on, even if desire keeps rewriting us in the future imperfect (we will have wanted, we will still be wanting), because your body is the grammar my solitude dreamed: a wild syntax of pulse and mercy, a parenthesis where the world can sleep. Let the angels keep their immaculate silence, let the ruined garden close its gates behind us; with your mouth near mine, I know love is a song beyond Eden.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an elegiac but life-affirming dedication to Robert Philen, opening with the thought that both speaker and addressee will die, “but not today.” Blend intimate declarations with dreamlike botanical and celestial imagery.
counterfactuals.output:
**For Robert Philen**

You will die, and I will die—but not today.

Today the morning vines are climbing through the windows,  
their green hands full of rain. Today the sun  
hangs like a lantern in the orchard,  
and every leaf is speaking your name.

I have loved you in the quiet ways:  
in cups left warm, in doors held open,  
in the small astonishment of finding you  
still here beneath the wheeling stars.

One night, the moon will gather us  
into its pale garden. Ferns will rise from our silence;  
wildflowers will borrow our breath.  
But not today.

Today, stand beside me.  
Let the roses burn without apology.  
Let the planets drift like seeds through the dark.  
We are mortal, Robert—  
and therefore radiant,  
and therefore here.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a dense, free-associative love poem about an unnamed “you” who is compared to strawberries, budding shrubs, lilies, asters, trillium, viburnum, snow, night, sleep, flowers, and the sea; portray that person as a dwelling when home is nowhere.
counterfactuals.output:
You are strawberries bruising their red grammar  
against my tongue, sweetness with a small green crown,  
the taste of June remembering itself in winter.  
You are budding shrubs at the edge of the vacant lot,  
each tight fist opening without argument;  
lilies lifting their pale lamps from the rain,  
asters speaking purple into the late-year air,  
trillium—threefold hush beneath the trees—  
viburnum foaming white along the ruined fence.

You are snow before footsteps,  
night before the first star admits it is burning,  
sleep with its dark hands untying the mind.  
You are flowers and the fever hidden in flowers,  
pollen, petal, stem, the soft insistence of roots;  
you are the sea entering every shell  
with one enormous, unfinishable sentence.

I move through you as wind through an orchard,  
as salt through blood, as moonlight through a room  
whose door has forgotten the wall.  
Where you touch me, distances fold:  
roads lose their names, maps loosen into birds,  
every exile grows a window.

And when home is nowhere—  
when the roof of the world blows off,  
when the keys in my pocket open only weather—  
you become the dwelling:  
your breath the curtains, your pulse the stair,  
your silence the table where I set down my hunger.  
I live there, unnamed beside you,  
while strawberries darken, asters close, snow falls,  
and the sea keeps carrying the night  
from room to room.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
